title: Farid of Pakpattan
hook: Sheikh Farid, a Sufi of the Punjab centuries before Nanak, whose Punjabi verses the Gurus treasured

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's saloks. Your line was sharp and short. Did one of the three come in handy? Today, a new voice, older than Kabir, older than the Gurus, and the first great poet of the Punjabi language. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

Every language has a first great voice, the one whose lines people still quote centuries later without always knowing where they came from. For Punjabi, the language of the Guru Granth Sahib's heartland, that voice belongs to a Muslim holy man who lived about three hundred years before Guru Nanak. His shrine still stands in a small town in what is now Pakistan, and people of every faith visit it. The Gurus kept his verses in their own book. Today, we meet him: Farid of Pakpattan.
screen: `EVERY LANGUAGE HAS A FIRST VOICE.` → `A SUFI, CENTURIES BEFORE NANAK.` → `KEPT IN THE GURUS' BOOK.`

segments.voice: Sheikh Farid, often called Baba Farid, lived in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. He was a Sufi, a Muslim mystic, of the Chishti order, known for its love of music and its welcome to the poor. He settled in a river town called Ajodhan, later renamed Pakpattan, and there he taught, fasted, prayed and fed whoever came. People called him Ganjshakar, treasury of sugar; there are many stories about why, and nobody can say which is true. What matters here is his language. The learned wrote in Persian or Arabic. Farid spoke to villagers in their own Punjabi, and his couplets are among the oldest poetry in the language. That's why people call him the first Punjabi voice. The Guru Granth Sahib holds four of his hymns and more than a hundred of his saloks. Sikh tradition says Guru Nanak met one of Farid's successors at Pakpattan and brought his verses home. Scholars honestly debate whether every salok is by Farid himself or partly by later Sheikhs of his line who used his name. Either way, the Gurus heard their own teaching in them. Here's one Sikhs love, in paraphrase: don't speak even one harsh word, for the True Lord lives in everyone. Don't break anyone's heart; every heart is a priceless jewel. A Muslim saint in a Sikh book, speaking the people's language about the jewel in every heart. It's hard to think of a better picture of truth having many singers.
screen: `BABA FARID — A CHISHTI SUFI.` · `AJODHAN, LATER PAKPATTAN.` · `THE PEOPLE'S OWN PUNJABI.` · `EVERY HEART, A PRICELESS JEWEL.` · then, large: `THE FIRST PUNJABI VOICE.`

segments.voice: Take Farid's line into the quiet: don't break anyone's heart; every heart is a priceless jewel. Say it slowly in your mind. Then picture one heart you might bruise today without meaning to: someone rushed, someone tired, someone who annoys you. See it as a jewel, easy to scratch, impossible to replace. Let the breath be soft. The bell holds the time.
Farid of Pakpattan. Baba Farid, the Chishti Sufi whose Punjabi couplets, among the oldest in the language, the Gurus placed in the Granth.
Your line: the first punjabi voice. Today, read or recall one line of Farid, the jewel in every heart, and let it guard your words once. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Farid's saloks and hymns are sung in Sikh kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib; his shrine at Pakpattan, in Pakistan's Punjab, is visited by people of many faiths.

fork.reveal: Farid spoke to ordinary people in their own Punjabi, and became the first great voice of the language.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Farid, an Arabic name meaning unique, matchless; his saloks begin fareedaa, O Farid.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Sikh scripture only has Sikh voices.
what it means: a Muslim Sufi who lived centuries before Guru Nanak speaks in the Granth, in the people's own Punjabi.

what a scholar hears: Fariduddin Ganjshakar (c. 1173–1266) of the Chishti order; four hymns and 112 saloks in the Granth, with debate over attribution to later Sheikhs such as Ibrahim, called Farid Sani.
